headings.title: Introduction to History Taking in Primary Health Care
headings.content: History taking forms the bedrock of clinical diagnosis in Nigerian primary health care settings. A thorough client interview often reveals up to eighty percent of diagnostic clues before any physical examination or laboratory investigation begins. Nurses must view this process not merely as an administrative data-gathering exercise, but as the initial phase of the therapeutic relationship. Effective communication builds trust, reduces patient anxiety, and uncovers vital details about the illness experience that simple lab tests might miss.

headings.title: Establishing Rapport and Communication Techniques
headings.content:
Creating a safe, welcoming environment encourages patients to share sensitive health information freely. Begin every interaction by greeting the patient respectfully using their preferred name or title. Non-verbal cues matter profoundly; maintain an open posture, nod encouragingly, and ensure appropriate eye contact while respecting cultural norms. 

- **Active listening**: Give the patient uninterrupted time to speak during the opening moments.
- **Open-ended questions**: Invite broad descriptions instead of short, closed answers.
- **Facification**: Use verbal prompts like "go on" or nods to keep the narrative flowing.
- **Empathy**: Acknowledge the patient's emotional state explicitly.

headings.title: Structuring the Patient Interview
headings.content:
A structured interview prevents the omission of critical clinical details while keeping the conversation focused. Experienced clinicians guide the flow from broad, open inquiries down to specific diagnostic details. Moving haphazardly between topics confuses the patient and yields disjointed records. 

1. **Introduction**: Greet the patient, introduce yourself, and explain the purpose of the talk.
2. **Presenting Complaint**: Identify the main reason for the hospital visit.
3. **History of Present Illness**: Explore the timeline, character, and aggravating factors of the main complaint.
4. **Past Medical History**: Review previous illnesses, surgeries, and chronic conditions.
5. **Family and Social History**: Assess hereditary risks and living conditions.
6. **Review of Systems**: Screen remaining body systems for hidden symptoms.

headings.title: Eliciting the Presenting Complaint and History of Present Illness
headings.content: The presenting complaint is recorded using the patient's own words whenever possible. Once established, the nurse expands this into the history of present illness. Mastering the mnemonic **SOCRATES** helps analyze pain or other symptoms systematically: Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associations, Time course, Exacerbating/relieving factors, and Severity. Avoid accepting vague descriptions; prompt the patient to clarify what they mean by terms like "stomach pain" or "heavy fever."

headings.title: Taking Past Medical, Surgical, and Family Histories
headings.content: Past medical history uncovers chronic conditions, previous hospital admissions, and infectious diseases like tuberculosis or malaria. Inquiring about past surgeries involves noting dates, indications, and any anesthetic complications. Family history focuses on first-degree relatives to identify inherited predispositions for conditions such as hypertension, diabetes mellitus, sickle cell disease, and malignancies. Always confirm the current health status or cause of death for parents and siblings.

headings.title: Assessing Social History and Environmental Factors
headings.content: Illness rarely occurs in a vacuum; social circumstances often dictate health outcomes. The social history explores occupation, housing conditions, water sources, sanitation, and travel habits. In Nigeria, inquiring about use of mosquito nets, biomass fuel exposure from firewood cooking, and alcohol or tobacco consumption is vital. Nurses must ask about these habits non-judgmentally to ensure the patient feels safe sharing accurate lifestyle details.

headings.title: Conducting a Systematic Review of Systems
headings.content:
The review of systems acts as a clinical safety net, uncovering symptoms the patient forgot to mention during the presenting complaint. Nurses screen major body systems sequentially, typically starting from the head and moving downwards to the feet. 

| Body System | Key Screening Questions | Common Findings |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cardiovascular | Chest pain, palpitations, orthopnea | Edema, dyspnea |
| Respiratory | Cough, sputum, wheezing, dyspnea | Hemoptysis |
| Gastrointestinal | Appetite changes, nausea, bowel habits | Heartburn, jaundice |
| Genitourinary | Dysuria, frequency, hematuria | Incontinence |

Ask simple, direct screening questions for each system while avoiding overly technical jargon.

headings.title: Documentation and Ethical Considerations in Patient Interviews
headings.content: Accurate, timely documentation transforms spoken interview data into a permanent legal and clinical record. Nurses must record objective findings clearly without incorporating personal biases or derogatory opinions. Maintaining patient confidentiality is an absolute ethical mandate; information shared during the interview must never be discussed outside professional contexts. Informed consent underpins every interaction, ensuring the patient understands why personal details are collected and how records are safeguarded.
